Overview — The Breast Cancer Framework
The commonest cancer in women. The framework: triple assessment to diagnose, receptor status (ER/PR/HER2) to treat, and TNM + NPI to prognosticate.
The three questions that drive everything: Is it cancer? (triple assessment) → What type + receptors? (histology) → How far + how aggressive? (staging / grade).
Cross-ref: benign breast disease (the differential cluster), screening / 2WW (next tab), and axillary surgery complications (lymphoedema).
Risk Factors — Mostly Oestrogen Exposure + Genetics

  • BRCA1 / BRCA2 — the key inherited cause
↑ Oestrogen exposure

  • Early menarche, late menopause

  • Obesity (peripheral oestrogen)
Other

  • Prior breast cancer

Pathological Types
  • Invasive ductal carcinoma (NST — no special type) = commonest
  • Invasive lobular carcinoma
  • DCIS (ductal carcinoma in situ) — pre-invasive; classic feature = comedo necrosis; seen as microcalcification on mammogram
  • LCIS (lobular carcinoma in situ)
  • Inflammatory breast cancer — progressive erythema + oedema (peau d'orange) without infection; aggressive, the key mimic of mastitis
  • Paget's disease of the nipple — nipple eczema/reddening → underlying malignancy

Metastasis sites — "2 Ls and 2 Bs": Lungs, Liver, Bones, Brain. Any metastatic tumour could have a breast primary.

Every suspicious breast lump gets all three components.

Staging & Prognosis
  • TNM (tumour, nodes, metastasis); all patients discussed at MDT
  • Gene-expression profiling (NICE DG34) for early ER+/HER2−/node− cancers → predicts recurrence risk + guides whether to add chemo
  • Nottingham Prognostic Index (NPI) — combines tumour size, nodal status and histological grade into good/moderate/poor groups
  • Grade: Scarff-Bloom-Richardson (tubule formation, nuclear pleomorphism, mitoses)
Treatment — Surgery → Adjuvant by Receptor/Node Status
Surgery (first-line)
  • Tumour <4 cm → wide local excision (WLE); larger/multifocal → mastectomy (± reconstruction)
  • Axilla: palpable nodes → axillary node clearance; impalpable → pre-op axillary USS ± biopsy: if positive → axillary node clearance; if negative → sentinel node biopsy
  • Axillary clearance risks arm lymphoedema + functional impairment
Radiotherapy: whole-breast radiotherapy for ALL women after wide local excision.

  • Metastatic/palliative: systemic therapy by receptor, bone-directed treatment, symptom control, MDT + supportive care (rehab, nurse counsellors, palliative input)

Overview — Triage & Triple Assessment
A differential cluster covering the non-cancerous causes of breast lumps, pain, nipple discharge and skin change. The skill examined is placing a breast symptom in the right box while always excluding cancer first — which is why triple assessment is the spine of the whole cluster, not any individual diagnosis.
The decisive first split is what is the presenting symptom — lump, pain, discharge or skin change — because each opens onto a different short differential and a different "cancer mimic" you must not miss. Cross-ref the Breast Cancer note (any suspicious finding routes to the 2WW pathway).

The Nipple Discharge Discriminator
📷 Image placeholder — Two-branch decision diagram — single-duct + bloody (± retroareolar nodule) → intraductal papilloma; multi-duct + green/brown → duct ectasia; any bloody discharge → investigate to exclude carcinoma.
Two questions resolve most nipple discharge: how many ducts, and is it bloody. A single duct + bloody discharge (± small retroareolar nodule) → intraductal papilloma; multi-duct + green/yellow/clear → duct ectasia. Any bloody discharge must be investigated to exclude carcinoma, even though the commonest cause (papilloma) is benign.

Overview
The commonest benign breast tumour in young women, typically 15–35. Localised proliferation of breast ducts and stroma, developing from a whole lobule — an "aberration of normal development" rather than a true neoplasm.
  • No meaningful increase in breast cancer risk
  • A significant proportion regress spontaneously over a few years
Clinical Features
  • A highly mobile, firm, smooth, well-defined, non-tender lump — so mobile it's nicknamed the "breast mouse" (slips away under the fingers)
  • Typically oval with well-defined margins; often multiple (simultaneously or sequentially)
Investigations
  • Triple assessment, as for any lump. On USS: a well-circumscribed, hypoechoic lesion with benign features
  • Core biopsy confirms the diagnosis — and biopsy confirmation removes the need for serial USS follow-up
Giant fibroadenoma (>5 cm) and the related phyllodes tumour (can be borderline/malignant, recurs locally) are the differentials for a large or rapidly growing lesion — don't assume benign without histology.
Management
  • Conservative is the default — reassurance + discharge (benign, tends to regress)
  • Surgical excision if >3 cm, enlarging, significantly symptomatic, or patient preference

Overview
Fluid-filled, epithelium-lined sacs — a common cause of a discrete lump in the perimenopausal years (~35–50). Hormonally driven, part of the fibrocystic spectrum.
  • Simple cysts carry no increased breast cancer risk
  • Caveat: a complex cyst (solid components / thick septations) warrants further assessment
Clinical Features
  • A smooth, mobile, sometimes tender lump; rubbery, often multiple
  • Can appear suddenly and fluctuate with the menstrual cycle; a tense cyst can be painful
Investigations
  • Triple assessment. USS: a simple cyst is anechoic (clean black fluid) with posterior acoustic enhancement — usually diagnostic
  • Mammography: a cyst can produce the characteristic radiolucent "halo sign"
A complex cyst (internal echoes, solid mural components) needs biopsy/aspiration cytology to exclude malignancy.
Management
  • Asymptomatic simple cysts — no treatment
  • Symptomatic → aspiration (diagnostic + therapeutic)
Two findings at aspiration trigger further investigation to exclude carcinoma: bloodstained aspirate, or a residual mass after aspiration → imaging + biopsy.

Overview
A benign, hormonally-driven condition: the breast becomes lumpy, nodular and often painful, fluctuating across the menstrual cycle. An exaggerated physiological response to cyclical hormones rather than a disease — hence much management is reassurance.
  • Middle reproductive years (~30–50); sits on the same spectrum as breast cysts (often coexist)
  • No increased breast cancer risk in its common (non-proliferative) form
Clinical Features
  • Lumpy, nodular breasts — often bilateral & diffuse rather than a single mass — with pain worse pre-menstrually, easing after menstruation
  • The nodularity is what brings the patient in → diagnose by triple assessment to exclude a discrete malignant lump, then reassure
Mastalgia
First step: distinguish true breast pain from chest-wall pain (costochondritis, musculoskeletal).
CyclicalNon-cyclical
TimingWorse pre-menstrually, eases after periodUnrelated to cycle
MechanismHormonal (fibrocystic)Duct ectasia, large pendulous breasts, referred chest-wall pain

Management of mastalgia: reassurance (most resolves), a well-fitted supportive bra, simple analgesia / topical NSAIDs. Severe refractory cyclical pain has specialist options (danazol, tamoxifen) — rarely needed at student level.

  • If imaging shows only diffuse fibrocystic change with no discrete lesion → reassure

Overview
Benign dilation + inflammation of the large central (sub-areolar) ducts, producing nipple discharge and sometimes retraction ("ectasia" = dilation). Ducts dilate and shorten with age (within ~3 cm of the nipple).
  • Classically perimenopausal / menopausal women; commoner in overweight women; associated with prior lactation
  • Significant overlap with periductal mastitis — often the same process
Clinical Features
  • Green, brown or creamy discharge, characteristically from multiple ducts — colour + multi-duct nature are the key benign signals (vs single-duct bloody papilloma)
  • Nipple retraction/inversion (periductal fibrosis) ± small sub-areolar lump — the retraction is what raises cancer concern
  • Smoking is a recognised risk factor (stronger for the periductal-mastitis end)
Investigations
  • Triple assessment, principally to exclude carcinoma — nipple retraction + discharge are also red flags for malignancy
  • Mammogram/USS; ductal assessment where discharge is bloody or single-duct
Management
  • No specific treatment if mild — reassurance once cancer excluded
  • Troublesome → surgical duct excision: microdochectomy (single-duct, preferred in younger women wishing to breastfeed) or total duct excision (older / multi-duct)
⭐ Exam Pearls
Perimenopausal + green-brown, multi-duct discharge ± retraction
= duct ectasia.
Benign mimic of cancer's nipple changes
Triple-assess to exclude malignancy (retraction is a shared red flag).
Smoking-associated
Overlaps with periductal mastitis.
Surgery if needed
Microdochectomy (young, single duct) vs total duct excision (older, multi-duct).
Overview
A benign warty tumour growing within a lactiferous (milk) duct, typically sub-areolar. Classic presentation: a single duct + bloody, sudden discharge ± small retroareolar nodule. Most commonly 35–55.
Benign — but because it presents with bloody nipple discharge (also cardinal for malignancy), it can never be assumed benign without investigation.
Clinical Features
  • Bloodstained (or clear/serous) discharge from a single duct — the hallmark and the key discriminator from duct ectasia's multi-duct green-brown discharge
  • Usually no palpable lump, unless large enough to form a small retroareolar nodule
Investigations
  • Triple assessment. Single-duct bloody discharge warrants ductal imaging (USS, ± ductography/ductoscopy) alongside mammography
  • Core/excision biopsy — a single-duct papilloma must be distinguished from DCIS, and atypia within a papilloma carries some malignant potential
Management
Microdochectomy — excision of the affected duct — is both diagnostic (histology to exclude malignancy) and therapeutic (resolves the discharge).
⭐ Exam Pearls
Single-duct, bloodstained discharge ± small/no nodule
= intraductal papilloma.
Benign cause of bloody discharge
But always excised (microdochectomy) to exclude carcinoma/DCIS.
The clean discriminator
Papilloma = single-duct, bloody; duct ectasia = multi-duct, green-brown.
Overview
Benign inflammatory process — damaged adipose tissue undergoes necrosis + fibrosis, producing a firm lump. Its whole importance: it is the classic benign mimic of carcinoma — a hard, irregular, fixed lump (± skin tethering) clinically and radiologically indistinguishable from cancer.
  • Typically obese women with large, pendulous breasts
  • Characteristically follows trauma — often trivial or unremembered (seatbelt, a knock, prior surgery/radiotherapy)
Clinical Features
  • Initially a firm, round lump; over time may organise into a hard, irregular, fixed lump ± skin tethering/dimpling — the features that mimic malignancy (usually painless)
  • A history of trauma/surgery supports it — but its absence doesn't exclude it
Investigations
Triple assessment is mandatory — you cannot distinguish fat necrosis from carcinoma clinically. Imaging may itself show suspicious features (spiculated mass, calcification), so core biopsy is critical to obtain histology and exclude malignancy.
Management
  • Once malignancy is confidently excluded on biopsy → conservative (typically resolves over time)
  • Excision only if it remains symptomatic or diagnostically uncertain

→ hard, irregular lump that mimics cancer.

Overview
An eczema-like change of the nipple that signals underlying breast malignancy — it looks benign but is associated with an underlying DCIS or invasive cancer in the great majority. Histologically: malignant (Paget) cells within the nipple epidermis.
A red flag masquerading as a benign nipple complaint — the trap is to treat it as eczema and miss the cancer.
Clinical Features & the Key Discriminator
📷 Image placeholder — Paget's vs nipple eczema — Paget's begins at the NIPPLE and spreads outward to the areola, whereas eczema begins at the areola and spares the nipple.
  • Reddening, thickening and scaling that begins at the NIPPLE and spreads to the areola, ± itching, ulceration or discharge
The classic discriminator (single most-tested point): Paget's starts at the nipple and spreads to the areola; nipple eczema starts at the areola and spares the nipple. A persistent unilateral nipple change is Paget's until proven otherwise.
Investigations
  • Biopsy of the nipple skin to confirm Paget cells
  • Mammography/USS to identify the underlying malignancy (DCIS or invasive), which co-exists in most cases — triple assessment principles apply
Management
  • Directed at the underlying breast cancer — surgery (mastectomy, or breast-conserving surgery with nipple excision depending on the disease) + appropriate adjuvant therapy (cross-ref Breast Cancer note)

BREAST__Breast Lump:
A breast lump is the commonest breast presentation, and the single question is whether it is cancer. Every discrete lump is worked up by triple assessment: clinical examination (P1–P5), imaging (ultrasound if <40, mammography ± ultrasound if ≥40; U1–U5 / M1–M5) and needle biopsy (core biopsy B1–B5, or FNA) — see breast cancer. Most lumps are benign: a fibroadenoma (young woman, firm, smooth, highly mobile — a “breast mouse”) or a breast cyst (perimenopausal, smooth, may be tender and fluctuant) — see benign breast disease. The task is to sort the discrete, hard, irregular or fixed lump — especially in an older woman, or with skin tethering, nipple change or an axillary node — from the reassuring one, using imaging and histology rather than clinical feel alone. Under NICE, a 2-week-wait suspected-cancer referral is made for an unexplained breast lump in anyone ≥30 (and for skin/nipple changes suggestive of cancer at any age).
🚨Assume a new discrete breast lump is cancer until triple assessment proves otherwise (see breast cancer). Refer under the 2-week-wait pathway any unexplained breast lump in a patient aged 30 or over, and consider urgent referral for those under 30 with concerning features. Red flags are a hard, irregular, fixed or tethered lump, skin dimpling or peau d’orange (see breast skin change), nipple retraction or bloody discharge (see nipple retraction, nipple discharge) and axillary lymphadenopathy. Never let a “normal” mammogram override a clinically suspicious lump — imaging can miss cancer, so proceed to biopsy. A tender, hot, fluctuant lump may be an abscess needing drainage, but a lump that does not settle must be biopsied to exclude inflammatory cancer (see painful red breast).

BREAST__Breast Pain (Mastalgia):
Breast pain (mastalgia) is very common and usually benign, but the job is to exclude the few serious causes. Most mastalgia is cyclical — bilateral, diffuse, upper-outer heaviness that worsens premenstrually and eases with menstruation, driven by hormonal change — or non-cyclical, a more constant, localised pain unrelated to the cycle (see benign breast disease). Crucially, much “breast” pain is actually chest-wall (extramammary) pain — costochondritis, Tietze’s, muscular strain or shingles — reproduced by palpating the chest wall rather than breast tissue. Isolated breast pain is rarely a symptom of cancer, but a focal, persistent pain with a lump or skin change must be assessed (see breast cancer). The two things not to miss are cardiac referred pain presenting as left-sided “breast” pain (see chest pain), and mastitis or an abscess in a red, tender breast (see painful red breast).
🚨Do not label pain as “mastalgia” without excluding cardiac pain. Left-sided or central chest pain radiating to the arm or jaw, worse on exertion, may be angina or an acute coronary syndrome masquerading as breast pain — assess with ECG and troponin (see chest pain, acute coronary syndrome). A focal, persistent pain with a palpable lump, skin dimpling or nipple change needs triple assessment to exclude cancer (see breast cancer). A hot, red, tender breast suggests mastitis or abscess — but inflammatory change that fails to settle must be biopsied (see painful red breast). Reassure the majority: cyclical and chest-wall pain are benign and respond to simple measures.

BREAST__Nipple Discharge:
Nipple discharge is sorted by its character, because a few patterns are worrying and most are not. The features that matter are blood, whether it is from a single duct or many, unilateral vs bilateral, and spontaneous vs expressed. Bloody or serosanguinous, single-duct, spontaneous, unilateral discharge is the red-flag pattern — think intraductal papilloma (the commonest cause) or, especially in older women or with a mass, DCIS / breast cancer (see breast cancer). At the other end, milky, bilateral, multi-duct discharge is galactorrhoea — usually physiological (pregnancy / lactation) or due to hyperprolactinaemia from drugs or a prolactinoma (see galactorrhoea, hyperprolactinaemia). Green, brown or cheesy, multi-duct discharge in a peri-/postmenopausal smoker is typically duct ectasia (see benign breast disease), and purulent discharge with a red tender breast suggests infection (see painful red breast).
🚨Bloody, single-duct, spontaneous, unilateral discharge is cancer until proven otherwise (see breast cancer). Assess with triple assessment and consider duct excision (microdochectomy / total duct excision) for diagnosis; an underlying papilloma or DCIS is common. A palpable lump with discharge raises the concern further. For milky bilateral discharge, exclude pregnancy, then check serum prolactin and thyroid function and review drugs; galactorrhoea with amenorrhoea, headache or visual-field loss suggests a prolactinoma needing pituitary MRI (see hyperprolactinaemia, galactorrhoea). Do not attribute a bloody unilateral discharge to “hormones”.

BREAST__Nipple Retraction / Inversion:
The single most useful question about a retracted nipple is: is it new? A new, unilateral nipple retraction — the nipple pulled in or slit-like — is a red flag for malignancy, caused by a tumour tethering and shortening the ducts, and is worked up with triple assessment (see breast cancer). It is even more concerning with a lump, skin dimpling, peau d’orange (see breast skin change) or an eczematous nipple suggesting Paget’s disease (see nipple eczema). The common benign cause is duct ectasia — a slit-like, transverse, often bilateral retraction in a peri-/postmenopausal smoker, frequently with green/brown multi-duct discharge (see benign breast disease). Longstanding or congenital inversion (present since puberty, bilateral, symmetrical) is benign, as is retraction from previous surgery, fat necrosis or periductal infection (see painful red breast).
🚨A newly retracted or inverted nipple is breast cancer until proven otherwise (see breast cancer). Refer under the 2-week-wait pathway and arrange triple assessment — do not attribute new unilateral retraction to ageing. Be especially alarmed by an associated lump, skin tethering, dimpling or peau d’orange (locally advanced or inflammatory cancer — see breast skin change), or a persistent eczematous nipple, which may be Paget’s disease and needs a nipple biopsy (see nipple eczema). By contrast, a longstanding, bilateral, symmetrical inversion is usually benign — but confirm it truly is longstanding.

BREAST__Breast Skin Change (Peau d'Orang:
Breast skin change — peau d’orange, tethering or dimpling — is a sinister sign that must be assumed malignant until proven otherwise. Peau d’orange (orange-peel dimpling with prominent hair follicles) reflects dermal lymphatic infiltration and oedema and is the hallmark of inflammatory breast cancer — a diffusely red, warm, swollen breast, often without a discrete lump, that comes on rapidly (see breast cancer). Skin tethering or dimpling (seen or accentuated on raising the arms) reflects a tumour pulling on the suspensory ligaments and signals a locally advanced cancer. The main benign mimics are mastitis or an abscess (a red, hot, tender segment that settles with antibiotics — see painful red breast), fat necrosis (dimpling after trauma/surgery — see benign breast disease) and eczema / dermatitis (itchy, scaly, often bilateral — see eczema / dermatitis).
🚨Peau d’orange and skin tethering are breast cancer until proven otherwise — refer urgently (see breast cancer). Inflammatory breast cancer is the great trap: a rapidly progressive red, swollen, warm breast with peau d’orange, frequently mimicking mastitis but with no discrete mass. The rule is simple — a red breast that does not settle within a short course of antibiotics must be biopsied (skin punch + core), never repeatedly re-treated as infection (see painful red breast). Look for tethering, dimpling, nodules or ulceration (locally advanced disease) and examine the axilla. Do not be reassured by the absence of a lump; in inflammatory cancer there often is none.

BREAST__Nipple Eczema (Paget's vs Eczema:
A scaly, red nipple forces one question: is it Paget’s disease or eczema? The distinction is made on pattern. Paget’s disease of the nipple is unilateral, begins on the nipple and spreads outward to the areola, and does not spare the nipple — a red, scaly, eczematous or crusted, sometimes eroded change that fails to resolve with topical steroids. It signifies an underlying malignancy (DCIS or invasive cancer) in the great majority (see breast cancer). Nipple eczema / dermatitis, by contrast, is usually bilateral, itchy, involves the areola but spares the nipple, and responds to emollients / topical steroid (see eczema / atopic dermatitis, contact dermatitis). The golden rule is simple: biopsy any nipple change that does not resolve — a persistent, unilateral, nipple-centred lesion is Paget’s until a nipple (punch) biopsy proves otherwise.
🚨Never treat a unilateral, persistent nipple rash as “eczema” indefinitely. Paget’s disease of the nipple is a red, scaly, eczematous or crusted change that starts at the nipple, is unilateral, and does not respond to topical steroid — it is associated with an underlying DCIS or invasive breast cancer in most cases (see breast cancer). A palpable lump is present in about half. The safe rule is to biopsy any nipple change persisting beyond a short trial of treatment (typically >2 weeks) with a nipple (punch) biopsy, and to arrange triple assessment to find the underlying cancer. Reassuring features for benign eczema are bilateral, itchy, areola-involving change that spares the nipple and clears with treatment (see eczema / atopic dermatitis).

BREAST__Painful Red Breast:
A painful, red breast is usually infection — but the diagnosis you cannot miss is inflammatory breast cancer. Most cases are mastitis: lactational (a breastfeeding woman with a wedge-shaped red, hot, tender area, fever and flu-like symptoms, from milk stasis and Staphylococcus aureus) or non-lactational / periductal (subareolar, in smokers, prone to recurrence and fistula). If pus collects, a breast abscess forms — a fluctuant, tender swelling needing ultrasound and aspiration / drainage. The trap is inflammatory breast cancer: a diffusely red, warm, swollen breast with peau d’orange, frequently without a discrete lump, that looks like mastitis but does not settle with antibiotics (see breast cancer, breast skin change). The governing rule is therefore simple: any red breast that fails to resolve on a short course of antibiotics must be biopsied. Also consider cellulitis (see cellulitis) and non-infective mimics.
🚨Do not keep treating a red breast as mastitis if it will not settle — biopsy it. Inflammatory breast cancer is the great mimic: a rapidly red, warm, swollen breast with peau d’orange and often no discrete mass, which is repeatedly misdiagnosed as recurrent mastitis (see breast cancer, breast skin change). After a short antibiotic course, a breast that has not resolved must have a skin punch + core biopsy. Meanwhile, do not undertreat sepsis: a fluctuant abscess needs ultrasound-guided aspiration or incision and drainage, and a systemically unwell patient needs prompt antibiotics ± admission. In lactational mastitis, encourage continued breastfeeding / expressing and give flucloxacillin.

BREAST__Axillary Lump:
An axillary lump is lymphadenopathy until proven otherwise, and the task is to sort benign nodes from malignant ones. Most axillary lumps are lymph nodes. Reactive / infective nodes are tender, mobile and follow a distal hand or arm infection or a systemic viral illness (see lymphadenopathy). The two malignant patterns to recognise are metastatic breast cancer — a hard, fixed ipsilateral node, often with a breast lump or an abnormal mammogram (see breast cancer) — and lymphoma — rubbery, painless nodes, frequently with night sweats, weight loss or itch and generalised lymphadenopathy (see lymphoma). Nodes may also drain a melanoma or skin cancer of the arm. The common non-nodal causes are a lipoma or sebaceous cyst (soft, mobile, subcutaneous — see skin lump / nodule) and hidradenitis suppurativa (recurrent painful abscesses and sinuses).
🚨A hard, fixed or persistent unexplained axillary node is malignant until proven otherwise. Examine the breast and the whole drainage territory (arm, hand, trunk skin) and both nodal basins. A hard ipsilateral node suggests metastatic breast cancer — arrange triple assessment and an ultrasound-guided node biopsy (see breast cancer). Rubbery, painless, generalised nodes with B symptoms (night sweats, weight loss, fever, itch) point to lymphoma, which needs an excisional lymph-node biopsy (FNA is insufficient) (see lymphoma, lymphadenopathy). Do not simply reassure a node that is hard, fixed, >2 cm, or persists beyond a few weeks — investigate it.

  • Tender, mobile node following a hand / arm infection, cat scratch or vaccination

  • Serology, imaging and biopsy as guided

  • Soft, mobile, subcutaneous lump (lipoma) or a cyst with a punctum (see skin lump / nodule)
  • Not a lymph node; benign
  • Clinical ± ultrasound; excise if troublesome

  • Hidradenitis suppurativa — recurrent painful abscesses, sinuses and scarring in the axilla
  • Accessory / axillary breast tissue (tail of Spence) — may enlarge cyclically
